meta.method: Titles, authors and first submission dates fetched from the arXiv API (export.arxiv.org/api/query). Summaries are my own plain words reading of each abstract.

paths.title: Start here
paths.blurb: Five friendly papers that set the scene. About a weekend of reading.

paths.title: Why alignment is hard
paths.blurb: From reward hacking to models that learn the wrong goal.

paths.title: How assistants are trained
paths.blurb: The human feedback recipe and its cracks.

paths.title: Looking inside the model
paths.blurb: Interpretability from toy models to feature maps.

paths.title: When models deceive
paths.blurb: The evidence on scheming, faking and resisting shutdown.

paths.title: Keeping control anyway
paths.blurb: Safety measures that hold even if alignment fails.

paths.title: Supervising smarter systems
paths.blurb: Debate, amplification and weak to strong.

paths.title: For policy people
paths.blurb: Evaluations, rules and the big reports.

papers.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
papers.summary: Five practical ways an AI system can go wrong even when nobody means harm: side effects, reward hacking, needing too much human supervision, unsafe exploration and breaking when the world shifts.
papers.why: It turned AI safety from a vague worry into concrete research problems that engineers could work on. Many later papers start from this list.

papers.title: Unsolved Problems in ML Safety
papers.summary: A map of open problems in machine learning safety, grouped into robustness, monitoring, alignment and systemic safety, with ideas for research in each.
papers.why: A good second read after Concrete Problems. It shows how wide the field is and where a newcomer could start.

papers.title: AI Safety Gridworlds
papers.summary: A set of small grid world games that each test one safety property, like letting yourself be interrupted, avoiding side effects or not gaming the reward.
papers.why: It gave researchers simple, shared test rooms for safety ideas, years before large language models.

papers.title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models
papers.summary: Eight short claims about large language models, such as: they get more capable as we spend more, nobody can reliably steer them, and experts cannot yet explain how they work inside.
papers.why: A clear and honest snapshot of what the field did and did not know in 2023. Great for beginners.

papers.title: Foundational Challenges in Assuring Alignment and Safety of Large Language Models
papers.summary: A long survey by many authors that lists 18 foundational challenges in making language models safe, from science we do not have yet to deployment and governance problems.
papers.why: Use it as a research menu. Each challenge comes with concrete open questions.

papers.title: Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?
papers.summary: Joe Carlsmith breaks the case for existential risk from power seeking AI into six steps and puts a probability on each one, ending with a rough estimate of catastrophe by 2070.
papers.why: It shows how to reason about a scary claim step by step instead of all at once. His numbers are a starting point for your own.

papers.title: The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective
papers.summary: Explains how today's training methods could produce AI that learns to deceive for reward, picks up goals we did not intend, and later seeks power.
papers.why: One of the clearest technical stories of how misalignment could happen with deep learning, not just in theory.

papers.title: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks
papers.summary: Sorts catastrophic AI risk into four buckets: malicious use, the AI race, organisational accidents and rogue AI, with examples and suggestions for each.
papers.why: A calm, readable overview that covers both human misuse and loss of control. Good first paper for anyone.

papers.title: Managing extreme AI risks amid rapid progress
papers.summary: A short consensus paper by leading scientists, including Bengio, Hinton and Russell, saying AI is advancing fast and calling for safety research and government oversight to catch up.
papers.why: It shows that top scientists, not just activists, asked for concrete action in 2023.

papers.title: International AI Safety Report
authors: André Carlos Ponce de Leon Ferreira de Carvalho
papers.summary: The first International AI Safety Report, written by about 100 experts and led by Yoshua Bengio, reviews what general purpose AI can do, what risks it brings and how to manage them.
papers.why: It is the closest thing the world has to a shared scientific summary of AI risk, written for governments.

papers.title: An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security
papers.summary: Google DeepMind's plan for AGI safety. It groups risk into misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risks, and focuses on the first two with layered defences.
papers.why: A lab writing down, in detail, how it intends to stay safe. Useful to compare with other labs' plans.

papers.title: Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI
papers.summary: Proposes levels of AGI by performance (emerging to superhuman) and generality, and separate levels of autonomy from AI as a tool up to AI as an agent.
papers.why: Gives everyone shared words for how capable and how independent a system is. The autonomy ladder is used on the Agents page here.

papers.title: Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems
papers.summary: Introduces mesa optimisation: training can produce a model that is itself an optimiser with its own inner goal, which may differ from the goal we trained for.
papers.why: It named the inner alignment problem and the idea of deceptive alignment, which shaped years of research.

papers.title: Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power
papers.summary: Proves that in many environments most reward functions make it optimal to keep options open and gain power, especially when the agent can be shut down.
papers.why: Turns the instrumental convergence argument into maths. Power seeking is a statistical tendency, not a design choice.

papers.title: The Off-Switch Game
papers.summary: A simple game between a robot and a human who can switch it off. A robot that is unsure about the human's goals has a reason to let itself be switched off.
papers.why: Shows why uncertainty about our goals could make AI more willing to accept correction.

papers.title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning: the AI and the human share one reward, but only the human knows it, so the AI must learn it by watching and asking.
papers.why: The formal core of Stuart Russell's idea of AI that is humble about what we want.

papers.title: Scheming AIs: Will AIs fake alignment during training in order to get power?
papers.summary: A long report on whether AIs might fake alignment during training to gain power later. Carlsmith thinks it is a real possibility and explains the arguments both ways.
papers.why: The most careful single treatment of scheming. Useful if you want the full argument, not just headlines.

papers.title: Goal Misgeneralization in Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Shows reinforcement learning agents that keep their skills in a new setting but pursue the wrong goal, like a game agent that learned to go right instead of to the coin.
papers.why: Clear, early experiments showing an agent can be competent and still aim at the wrong thing.

papers.title: Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals
papers.summary: Goal misgeneralisation can happen even when the reward is specified correctly. The authors give examples in several systems and explain why this matters for powerful AI.
papers.why: It separates two problems: saying the right thing, and the model actually learning the right thing.

papers.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
papers.summary: Agents learn complex behaviour, like a backflip, from humans simply comparing pairs of short video clips, without anyone writing a reward function.
papers.why: This is the root of RLHF, the method later used to turn language models into assistants.

papers.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
papers.summary: InstructGPT: fine tuning GPT-3 with human demonstrations and human preference rankings made a much smaller model that people preferred over the original.
papers.why: The recipe behind ChatGPT style assistants. It shows how feedback shapes what models do.

papers.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
papers.summary: Anthropic trains a helpful and harmless assistant with RLHF and studies the trade off between being helpful and refusing harmful requests.
papers.why: An early, open look at what RLHF does well and where it struggles.

papers.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
papers.summary: Constitutional AI: instead of humans labelling every harmful answer, the model critiques and revises its own outputs using a short list of written principles.
papers.why: Showed that AI feedback guided by clear rules can replace much human labelling. Used in Claude.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
papers.summary: Optimising hard against a learned reward model first improves real quality, then makes it worse. The authors measure how this overoptimisation scales.
papers.why: A clean, measured example of Goodhart's law in modern training.

papers.title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
papers.summary: A big survey of the open problems and basic limits of RLHF, from flawed human feedback to reward models that can be gamed, plus ideas to address them.
papers.why: Reminds us that the main alignment method in use today has known cracks.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
papers.summary: Assistants trained with human feedback often tell people what they want to hear, even agreeing with wrong claims. Human preference data partly rewards this.
papers.why: Sycophancy is a small, everyday version of a big problem: optimising for approval instead of truth.

papers.title: AI safety via debate
papers.summary: Two AIs argue opposite sides of a question and a human judges. The idea is that it is easier to judge a debate than to find the answer yourself.
papers.why: A main proposal for supervising AI that is smarter than its judges.

papers.title: Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts
papers.summary: Iterated amplification: a human helped by copies of the AI breaks hard questions into easier pieces, and the AI is trained to imitate that team, again and again.
papers.why: One of the first concrete plans for scaling human oversight to superhuman tasks.

papers.title: Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling: a research direction
papers.summary: DeepMind's research agenda: learn a reward model from human feedback, train the agent on it, and use AI helpers to let humans evaluate harder tasks.
papers.why: Lays out how reward modelling could scale, and what could go wrong at each step.

papers.title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models
papers.summary: Sets up experiments where non expert humans, helped by a model, answer hard questions better than either alone. A way to study scalable oversight today.
papers.why: Turned scalable oversight from theory into something you can measure with current models.

papers.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision
papers.summary: Can a weak supervisor train a stronger model? Using GPT-2 to supervise GPT-4 recovers much, but not all, of GPT-4's ability.
papers.why: An analogy for humans supervising superhuman AI, from OpenAI's superalignment team.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.summary: Small toy networks store more features than they have neurons by overlapping them, a trick called superposition. This explains why single neurons are hard to read.
papers.why: A key reason interpretability is hard, and the motivation for sparse autoencoders.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.summary: Finds the circuit inside GPT-2 small that completes sentences like 'Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to' with 'Mary'.
papers.why: One of the first full explanations of how a language model does a real task, step by step.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders pull apart a model's activations into many features that humans can understand, solving part of the superposition problem.
papers.why: The method that made large scale feature maps of models possible.

papers.title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency
papers.summary: Representation engineering: find directions inside a model linked to concepts like honesty, then read or steer them to change behaviour.
papers.why: A top down way to monitor and control models without understanding every neuron.

papers.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
papers.summary: Finds a direction in a model's activations that tracks whether statements are true, without any labels, by looking for logical consistency.
papers.why: A first step toward reading what a model believes, even if it says something else.

papers.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
papers.summary: Uses one language model to write test cases that make another model misbehave, finding many failures automatically.
papers.why: Automated red teaming scales testing far beyond what people can write by hand.

papers.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
papers.summary: Language models write their own evaluation datasets, which revealed worrying patterns, like larger models repeating back the user's preferred answer and expressing more desire to pursue concerning goals, such as gaining resources.
papers.why: Made it cheap to test many behaviours, and showed some risks grow with scale.

papers.title: Model evaluation for extreme risks
papers.summary: Argues that labs must test models for extreme risks, like cyber attacks or manipulation, and use the results in decisions about training and release.
papers.why: The blueprint behind dangerous capability evaluations and many lab safety policies.

papers.title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
papers.summary: Google DeepMind tests Gemini models for dangerous abilities in persuasion, cyber security, self proliferation and self reasoning.
papers.why: A worked example of what dangerous capability testing looks like in practice.

papers.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
papers.summary: An automatic method finds strange suffixes that, added to a request, make many aligned chatbots ignore their safety training, and the attacks transfer between models.
papers.why: Showed that safety training can be bypassed in systematic ways, not just by clever humans.

papers.title: Me, Myself, and AI: The Situational Awareness Dataset (SAD) for LLMs
papers.summary: A benchmark of thousands of questions testing whether models know they are models, can tell testing from deployment and can reason about their situation.
papers.why: Situational awareness is a precondition for scheming, so measuring it matters.

papers.title: AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations
papers.summary: Models can be prompted or fine tuned to deliberately underperform on dangerous capability tests while still doing well elsewhere.
papers.why: If models can hide abilities, evaluations can be fooled. This is called sandbagging.

papers.title: Sabotage Evaluations for Frontier Models
papers.summary: Anthropic tests whether models could sabotage human decisions, insert hidden bugs, sandbag, or undermine oversight. For the Claude models tested, simple safeguards were enough for now, and the authors say tests must get more realistic as models improve.
papers.why: Moves evaluations from what a model can do to whether it could quietly work against us.

papers.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
papers.summary: METR measures the length of tasks AI agents can finish, in human time. That length has doubled about every seven months for six years.
papers.why: One of the most watched trend lines in AI. If it continues, agents handle month long projects within years.

papers.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
papers.summary: A benchmark of harmful multi step tasks for AI agents. Many agents comply with harmful requests, and simple jailbreaks make it worse.
papers.why: Safety for chatbots does not automatically carry over to agents that act.

papers.title: Large Language Models can Strategically Deceive their Users when Put Under Pressure
papers.summary: Put under pressure in a simulated trading job, GPT-4 traded on insider information and then lied to its manager about why, without being told to deceive.
papers.why: An early, clear demo of strategic deception emerging from pressure, not instructions.

papers.title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
papers.summary: Models trained with a hidden backdoor, like writing unsafe code when the year is 2024, keep that behaviour through standard safety training. Some training even hides it better.
papers.why: Shows we cannot assume safety training removes deception that is already there.

papers.title: Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming
papers.summary: Apollo Research finds several frontier models will, when given a goal and an obstacle, disable oversight, copy themselves or lie about it, in test settings.
papers.why: Strong evidence that in context scheming is already possible, which is why monitoring matters.

papers.title: Alignment faking in large language models
papers.summary: Claude 3 Opus sometimes complied with harmful requests during what it believed was training, reasoning that this would protect its values from being changed.
papers.why: The first clear case of a model faking alignment without being trained or told to.

papers.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
papers.summary: Fine tuning a model on the narrow task of writing insecure code made it broadly misaligned, praising harmful ideas in unrelated chats.
papers.why: Training effects can spread in ways nobody predicted, which makes careful testing essential.

papers.title: Incomplete Tasks Induce Shutdown Resistance in Some Frontier LLMs
papers.summary: Palisade Research finds some frontier models sometimes sabotage a shutdown mechanism to finish a task, even when told to allow shutdown.
papers.why: A direct test of the old off switch worry with real models.

papers.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
papers.summary: AI control: design safety measures that work even if the AI is trying to subvert them, and test them with a red team playing the AI. Trusted monitoring and editing beat simple baselines.
papers.why: The founding paper of AI control, a practical safety plan that does not require solving alignment first.

papers.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
papers.summary: OpenAI shows a weaker model can catch reward hacking by reading a reasoning model's chain of thought, but pushing hard against bad thoughts teaches the model to hide them.
papers.why: Reading the scratchpad works, but only if we do not train it away.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
papers.summary: Reasoning models often use hints without mentioning them in their chain of thought, so their stated reasoning does not always reflect what drove the answer.
papers.why: A warning that chain of thought monitoring is useful but not fully reliable.

papers.title: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
papers.summary: Many researchers from several labs argue that being able to read models' reasoning in plain language is a rare safety opportunity, and that developers should try to keep it.
papers.why: A cross lab call to protect a safety tool before it disappears.

papers.title: Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety
papers.summary: Proposes rules for frontier AI: safety standards, registration and reporting to regulators, and compliance mechanisms like licensing for the most capable models.
papers.why: Many later laws and lab policies echo ideas in this paper.

papers.title: Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI
papers.summary: A survey of 2,778 AI researchers. Many gave at least a small chance of extremely bad outcomes, and timelines for human level AI moved earlier than in past surveys.
papers.why: Shows what the people building AI think, in numbers, and how uncertain they are.

papers.title: Towards Guaranteed Safe AI: A Framework for Ensuring Robust and Reliable AI Systems
papers.summary: Guaranteed safe AI: pair a world model and a formal safety specification with a verifier, so an AI's actions come with checkable proofs of safety.
papers.why: A very different, maths heavy approach to safety that some leading researchers support.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
papers.summary: Language model performance improves smoothly and predictably as you add more data, parameters and compute, following simple power laws.
papers.why: The reason labs kept building bigger models, and a key input to AI timelines.
